people.name: Ada Jones
people.summary: English-born American vaudeville singer, the most recorded woman of the acoustic era and the reigning comic soprano of the wax Amberol catalogue.
people.biography:
Ada Jones was born in Lancashire and brought to Philadelphia as a child. She began making records in the brown-wax era and by 1905 was the busiest female recording artist in the United States, working for Edison, Victor, Columbia and half a dozen smaller firms at once. Her voice was bright, forward and slightly nasal — precisely the qualities that survived the acoustic horn — and she had an unusual gift for character work, moving between Irish colleen, Bowery girl, small-town flirt and stage-Chinese or stage-Black caricature within a single month's releases.

On the four-minute wax Amberols she is everywhere, alone and in the celebrated duet partnership with Billy Murray. The extra two minutes suited her: it gave room for the spoken asides and the third and fourth verses that a two-minute Gold Moulded had to cut. Her health failed in the 1920s and she died on tour in Rocky Mount, North Carolina, in 1922.

people.name: Billy Murray
people.summary: The most popular male recording artist in America between roughly 1905 and 1915, and the definitive voice of Tin Pan Alley on cylinder.
people.biography:
Born in Philadelphia to Irish immigrant parents and raised in Denver, Billy Murray came off the vaudeville stage into the studios around 1903 and stayed for four decades. His diction was the reason: every consonant landed, and on a wax cylinder played through a small horn in a parlour that mattered more than beauty of tone. He was known in the trade as the Denver Nightingale.

Murray recorded for every major company, so the same song often exists in near-simultaneous Edison, Victor and Columbia versions. On the wax Amberols he appears as a solo comic tenor, as the lead of the American Quartet, and — most memorably — opposite Ada Jones in a run of conversational duets that are still the best-known records of the period.

people.name: Arthur Collins
people.summary: American baritone billed as "The King of Ragtime Singers"; with Byron G. Harlan he formed the most heavily recorded duet team of the cylinder era.
people.biography:
Collins built his career on the so-called coon song, the ragtime-adjacent genre of the 1890s and 1900s in which white performers sang in heavy Black dialect. He was extremely good at it by the standards his industry applied, and extremely prolific, which means a very large share of the surviving cylinder repertoire carries material a modern listener will find offensive. That is a fact about the catalogue rather than a reason to pretend the records do not exist.

His partnership with the tenor Byron G. Harlan ran from about 1901 to the mid-1920s. Collins took the low line and the comic dialect; Harlan took the melody and the sentiment. Collins was badly injured in a fall through a stage trap in 1921 and never fully recovered.

people.name: Byron G. Harlan
people.summary: American tenor, Arthur Collins's duet partner and a specialist in sentimental "mother and home" ballads as well as rube comedy.
people.biography: Harlan came to records from the concert and minstrel circuit and had a light, plaintive tenor that Edison's engineers liked. Alone he sang tearful ballads about dying children and absent mothers; with Collins he sang ragtime duets and dialect comedy. The pairing was so commercially reliable that Edison, Victor and Columbia all kept them under contract simultaneously for years.

people.name: Will Oakland
people.summary: American countertenor whose unusually high male voice made him a favourite for old-time and sentimental songs on cylinder.
people.biography: Oakland sang in a true high countertenor rather than falsetto, a sound that carried well through the recording horn and was marketed as a novelty in its own right. He recorded prolifically for Edison in the Amberol years, usually in nostalgic parlour material, and later ran nightclubs in New York.

people.name: Walter Van Brunt
people.summary: American tenor who began recording for Edison as a teenager and became one of the house voices of the late wax Amberol and early Blue Amberol period.
people.biography: Van Brunt was still in his teens when Edison began using him regularly, and his clear, unforced tenor is all over the catalogue from about 1910. In the 1920s he adopted the stage name Walter Scanlan and worked in Irish-American musical theatre; records under both names are the same singer and are catalogued here as one person.

people.name: Elizabeth Spencer
people.summary: American soprano and one of Edison's most-used house singers in the Amberol and Diamond Disc years, particularly in sacred and sentimental repertoire.

people.name: Albert Campbell
people.summary: American tenor, a fixture of quartet and duet recording from the 1890s to the 1920s and a founding member of the Peerless Quartet.

people.name: Henry Burr
people.summary: Canadian-born ballad tenor, the great sentimental voice of the acoustic era; on Edison he was usually billed under the pseudonym Irving Gillette.
people.biography: Burr recorded under a startling number of names because he was under contract to several companies at once. Edison generally issued him as Irving Gillette. He specialised in the slow, sincere ballad — the kind of song that sold steadily for twenty years — and by his own later account made several thousand records.

people.name: Frank C. Stanley
people.summary: American bass-baritone and banjoist, ubiquitous in quartets and duets until his early death in December 1910.

people.name: Harry Lauder
people.summary: Scottish music-hall comedian and singer, the highest-paid variety performer in the world before the First World War and Edison's most valuable British artist.
people.biography: Lauder built an international career on a stage-Scot persona — kilt, crooked stick, broad Lanarkshire patter — and songs he largely wrote himself. His Edison cylinders were recorded in London and issued in the British 12000 four-minute series, with many of them also sold in America. He was knighted in 1919 for his wartime entertainment and fundraising work.

people.name: Sousa's Band
people.summary: John Philip Sousa's professional touring band, whose recordings were usually made under an assistant conductor rather than Sousa himself.

people.name: United States Marine Band
people.summary: The President's Own, the oldest continuously active professional musical organisation in the United States, and a recording band for Edison in the cylinder era.

people.name: New York Military Band
people.summary: An Edison studio band name used for pick-up groups of New York players; one of the most frequently credited ensembles on Amberol and Blue Amberol cylinders.

people.name: Edison Military Band
people.summary: Edison's own house military band, credited on a large share of the earliest wax Amberol releases.

people.name: National Military Band
people.summary: Edison's London studio band, credited on the British-recorded band titles that circulated in the American Amberol lists as the National (London) Military Band.

people.name: Edison Mixed Quartet
people.summary: Edison's house mixed-voice quartet, used chiefly for sacred and old-favourite material.

people.name: Knickerbocker Quartette
people.summary: An Edison male quartet name; the personnel most often cited are Harry Anthony, Walter Van Brunt, James F. Harrison and William F. Hooley.

people.name: American Symphony Orchestra
people.summary: The name Edison gave to the studio orchestra at West Orange for light-classical and show-selection recordings.

people.name: Empire Vaudeville Co.
people.summary: An Edison house billing for the mixed casts assembled to record vaudeville sketches with music.

people.name: Frieda Hempel
people.summary: German coloratura soprano, a Metropolitan Opera star of the 1910s who recorded exclusively for Edison from 1917 and became the leading name of the Royal Purple series.
people.biography: Hempel sang at the Berlin Court Opera and then at the Metropolitan from 1912, where she was celebrated as the Queen in Les Huguenots and as the Marschallin in the American premiere of Der Rosenkavalier. In the later 1910s she built a second career giving Jenny Lind centenary concerts in period costume, and her Edison repertoire reflects that turn towards simple ballads and old favourites as much as towards opera.

people.name: Criterion Quartet
people.summary: An Edison male quartet of the late 1910s, used repeatedly to back celebrity soloists on Diamond Disc and Royal Purple issues.

people.name: Alessandro Bonci
people.summary: Italian lyric tenor of the generation of Caruso, admired above all for elegance of line; his Edison cylinders open the 29000 celebrity block.
people.biography: Bonci made his debut in Parma in 1896 and was quickly set up by press and public as the refined alternative to Caruso's weight and heat. He sang at Covent Garden, La Scala, the Manhattan Opera House and the Metropolitan. His Edison cylinders are prized by collectors both for the singing and for their place at the head of the company's celebrity numbering.

people.name: Albert Spalding
people.summary: The first American-born violinist to win a major international reputation, and an Edison exclusive artist during the Diamond Disc years.

records.title: New colonial marches
records.description:
A band record from the very first months of the four-minute wax Amberol, when Edison was filling the new series as fast as the West Orange studio could cut masters. The Edison Military Band was the company's own house ensemble, and marches were the obvious material for a format whose selling point was that it held twice as much music: a two-minute cylinder could take a march at speed with one strain trimmed, while four minutes allowed the trio and the repeat to stand as written.

The Amberol experiment began in the autumn of 1908. Edison had cut the groove pitch from 100 to 200 threads to the inch, which doubled playing time on the same size of cylinder but demanded a finer reproducer stylus and a slower feed screw. Existing phonographs needed a conversion kit, and dealers spent 1909 fitting them. A record numbered 50 belongs to that scramble.

Because this is a black wax pressing rather than celluloid, it is soft. The 200-thread groove is roughly half the width of a Gold Moulded groove, so a two-minute reproducer dropped on it by mistake ploughs the wall out in a single pass — the commonest way these records died. A good copy shows an even matte sheen across the surface with no bright, polished band where a wrong stylus has ridden.
records.notes: The title as transcribed by the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive reads as a plural; the underlying piece is the familiar colonial march material of the period. Treat the exact printed title wording as unconfirmed.

links.label: Edison Amberol 50 at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive

records.title: The traveling salesman
records.credit_line: Vaudeville sketch with song and banjo
records.description:
One of the small comic playlets that the four-minute cylinder made commercially possible. A sketch needs time to set a scene, land two or three gags and finish with a song; on a two-minute Gold Moulded there was room for the gags or the song but rarely both. Edison's answer was the Amberol, and records like this one — dialogue, a banjo, and a chorus at the end — are the format arguing for itself.

The Empire Vaudeville Co. was not a touring troupe but a house billing, the name Edison put on whatever combination of studio regulars was assembled for a given sketch. The traveling salesman was a stock American comic type long before Willy Loman: brash, over-familiar, forever arriving in a small town with a case of samples and designs on the landlady's daughter.

For a collector, sketch cylinders are worth hunting because they preserve spoken performance styles that no other medium of 1909 recorded. They are also among the hardest wax Amberols to find in playable condition, because a talking record with a laugh at the end got played to death in the parlour.
records.notes: Spoken-word wax Amberols suffer badly from surface bloom and mould; the greasy grey film that develops on stored black wax attacks the groove wall itself. Never wash a wax Amberol — water and detergent both damage the surface permanently.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Dance of the hours
records.subtitle: La gioconda
records.description:
Ponchielli's ballet from the third act of La Gioconda, arranged for military band. In 1909 this was simply a popular concert number, one of the pieces every band in America could play; its later career as cartoon shorthand for elephants in tutus was thirty years away.

The piece is a good illustration of why Edison built the Amberol at all. Played complete it runs well past two minutes, so the Gold Moulded catalogue could only offer it cut. Four minutes let a band take the whole sequence of dances at something like concert tempo, and Edison's advertising leaned hard on exactly that argument.

This title was carried forward into the celluloid era, appearing later in the Blue Amberol series as number 2171. Cross-issues like this are common and useful: where a wax Amberol is unfindable or unplayable, the Blue Amberol reissue often preserves the same performance in a far more durable material.
records.notes: Reissued on Blue Amberol 2171. The wax original is the scarcer of the two by a wide margin.

records.title: I'm awfully strong for you
records.description:
Billy Murray with chorus, in the mode that made him the best-selling male singer in America: a bright, fast, front-of-the-beat delivery of a Tin Pan Alley courtship song, every syllable audible.

The chorus behind him is the usual Edison expedient — two or three studio singers crowded round the horn — and it exists to give the last refrain a lift rather than to add harmony of any subtlety. What matters is Murray's timing. He sings slightly ahead of the orchestra throughout, which on a small parlour phonograph reads as energy rather than haste.

A record from 1909 is an early Amberol, and early Amberols are the ones most likely to have been played on hastily converted machines by owners who had not quite understood that the reproducer had to be changed as well as the feed screw. Check the groove under a loupe before playing anything from the first few hundred numbers.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Cuddle up a little closer, lovey mine
records.description:
Karl Hoschna's melody to Otto Harbach's lyric, introduced in the 1908 musical The Three Twins and one of the biggest song hits of its year. It is a genuinely good tune — a lazy, syncopated descent that sounds more like 1925 than 1908 — and it has stayed in circulation ever since.

Edison's version puts Ada Jones and Billy Murray together with a small supporting company, which is the arrangement that made both of them famous. The two had a knack for sounding like a real couple bickering their way towards agreement: Jones arch and a little suspicious, Murray coaxing. The spoken exchanges between verses are the point of the record, and they are exactly what the extra two minutes of the Amberol format bought.

Collectors should expect this one to have been played hard. It was a hit song in a hit format at a moment when most owners had precisely one four-minute reproducer, correctly fitted or not, and the wax is unforgiving of a single wrong pass.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: The debutante waltz
records.description:
A concert waltz played by the United States Marine Band, one of the ensembles Edison used to give the Amberol catalogue institutional weight. The Marine Band's name on a record label in 1909 carried the same implication it does now — official, disciplined, American — and Edison used it accordingly.

The waltz was the form that benefited most obviously from four minutes. A concert waltz is built as a chain of strains with an introduction and a coda that gathers them up again; cut to two minutes it becomes a fragment. At Amberol length the shape survives.

Band records of this period are also, in practice, the wax Amberols most likely to be found in decent condition. They were bought for the parlour phonograph rather than for the children, and a march or waltz got fewer repeat plays than a comic song.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Old comrades march
records.description:
Carl Teike's Alte Kameraden, written in the 1880s and by 1909 one of the most played marches in the world — a German regimental march that had become international property, and a standard for American concert bands alongside Sousa's own.

The United States Marine Band reading is straight and unhurried, with the trio taken at full length. The march's celebrated countermelody in the trio is the reason bandsmen love it, and it is the passage that a two-minute cylinder would have had to sacrifice.

Teike wrote the piece, according to the durable story, after being told there was no room for him in his own regimental band; it has outlasted the regiment. On cylinder it is a useful demonstration record, because the four-minute format lets you hear a full march played as a band would actually play it on a bandstand.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: The bird on Nellie's hat
records.description:
Alfred Solman's tune to Arthur Lamb's lyric, published in 1906 and one of Ada Jones's signature numbers. The conceit is that the stuffed bird on a young woman's hat has watched her whole courtship and is in a position to comment; the joke belongs to the era of the plume trade, when whole birds really were mounted on millinery and the Audubon societies were campaigning against it.

Jones plays it with the timing of a stage comedienne, letting the bird's punchlines sit for a beat. The song had already been recorded on two-minute cylinders; the four-minute Amberol let the later verses stand, and the joke depends on accumulation, so the longer version is the better one.

By 1909 Jones was the most recorded woman in the United States, and this is the kind of record that made her so — a strong lyric idea, delivered by a voice that cut through the acoustic horn without strain.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Selection from "Woodland"
records.description:
A medley from Gustav Luders's 1904 musical comedy Woodland, played by the American Symphony Orchestra — Edison's name for the studio orchestra at West Orange rather than any concert body.

Woodland was a curiosity even in its own day: an operetta in which the entire cast plays birds, with a plot of avian court intrigue. Luders, a German-born Milwaukee composer, had a real hit with The Prince of Pilsen a year earlier, and Woodland rode on it. The score's best numbers survived as band and orchestra selections long after the show closed.

Selection records were a staple of the Amberol catalogue because they solved the format's central problem: what do you put on four minutes that does not simply mean playing a two-minute piece twice. A medley of four or five themes from a show fitted the length exactly, and let a family who had never been to New York hear most of the score.

links.label: Edison Amberol Record 238 in the Lehigh University Libraries exhibit

records.title: Crown diamonds
records.subtitle: Overture
records.description:
Auber's overture to Les diamants de la couronne, recorded in London by the band Edison billed in the American lists as the National (London) Military Band.

The opera itself had largely left the stage by 1909, but its overture had not: like the overtures to Poet and Peasant and Light Cavalry it had become a bandstand warhorse, played by every municipal and regimental band in Europe and America. Recording it at four minutes meant the whole piece could be issued rather than a truncated arrangement.

Edison's London studio supplied a steady flow of band and music-hall masters to the American catalogue, which is why a collector working through a run of wax Amberols keeps meeting British ensembles. The British-recorded titles are often marginally better balanced than the West Orange band records of the same date, the London engineers having had more practice at getting a full band into one horn.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Stars and stripes forever march
records.description:
Sousa's Band playing Sousa's march — the piece he wrote on the boat home from Europe at Christmas 1896 and which Congress made the national march of the United States in 1987.

A caution that matters for this and every other Sousa's Band record of the period: the band recorded far more often than Sousa conducted it. Studio dates were normally taken by an assistant, most often Arthur Pryor in the earlier years and Herbert L. Clarke later, while Sousa himself was on tour and in any case thought recording an inferior way to hear a band. The label credit is to the organisation, not to the man.

At four minutes the march gets its full architecture: the two opening strains, the famous trio with the piccolo obbligato, the grandioso return with trombone countermelody. This is the reading that convinced a lot of Edison customers to pay for the Amberol conversion, and it remains one of the more commonly encountered wax Amberols — which is fortunate, because it is also one of the more commonly ruined ones.
records.notes: A very heavily played title. Look for an even surface with no polished band; a copy that sounds shrill and thin at the start of the record has usually been tracked with a two-minute reproducer at some point in its life.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Lead kindly light
records.description:
John Henry Newman's hymn of 1833, written during a becalmed sea crossing off Sardinia, sung to John Bacchus Dykes's tune Lux Benigna. It was among the most popular hymns in the English-speaking world for a century, and it sold steadily on record for as long as the parlour phonograph lasted.

Edison's Knickerbocker Quartette was one of several house names for the company's male quartet, the personnel usually given as Harry Anthony, Walter Van Brunt, James F. Harrison and William F. Hooley. Sacred quartet records were a fixed part of every monthly supplement, aimed squarely at the Sunday use of a machine bought for weekday entertainment.

The recording is close and dry, four voices around one horn with no accompaniment competing for the groove — which is why quartet cylinders of this period often sound better than the orchestral ones beside them.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: I will sing the wondrous story
records.description:
Francis Rowley's gospel hymn of 1886, set to Peter Bilhorn's tune, sung by Edison's house mixed quartet. Revival hymnody of this kind — written for American camp meetings and city missions rather than for cathedral choirs — was enormously popular on cylinder, and Edison issued it in quantity.

A mixed quartet gave the engineers a problem and an opportunity: four voices spanning soprano to bass covered more of the usable frequency range than any single singer, and the resulting records are often the best-sounding things in a month's list. The opportunity was taken; the balance here is careful, with the women set slightly back from the horn.

Sacred cylinders tend to survive in better condition than comic ones, having been played on Sundays rather than at parties. They are correspondingly less sought after, which makes them one of the cheapest ways into genuine wax Amberol collecting.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: I'm glad I'm a boy and I'm glad I'm a girl
records.description:
A Jones and Murray duet in their standard mode: two children comparing the advantages of their respective sexes, with the adult joke running just under the surface for the benefit of the parents in the room.

The child-voice duet was a genre of its own in 1909, and both singers were expert at it. Jones pitches up into a small girl's register without going shrill; Murray produces a boy's flat, argumentative delivery that carries the comedy. The orchestra stays out of the way, which on a wax cylinder is the difference between hearing the words and not.

Material like this is where the wax Amberol repertoire feels furthest from later cylinder collecting. The Blue Amberols of the 1920s are dance bands and Irish tenors; the wax Amberols of 1909 are music hall on a shellac budget, and their humour is often as dated as their surface is fragile.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: The rifle regiment march
records.description:
Another Sousa march, written in 1886 for the Third Regiment of the United States Army and here played by the Marine Band — the organisation Sousa himself had led from 1880 to 1892 and for which he wrote much of his early work.

The Rifle Regiment is early Sousa and sounds it: tighter, more compact and less flamboyant than the marches of the following decade, with a brisk trio that does not linger. It is the kind of piece that fills out a supplement rather than headlining one, and the wax Amberol catalogue is largely built of such pieces.

For the collector these mid-list band records are the workhorses of a wax Amberol collection. They turn up in dealer boxes, they are rarely expensive, and a clean one demonstrates what the format could do better than any famous title that has been played a thousand times.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Lyna! Oh! Oh! Miss Lyna!
records.description:
Collins and Harlan in the genre that made them, and which makes a large part of the wax Amberol catalogue difficult listening today. The coon song was a commercial category of American popular music from roughly 1890 to 1915: comic songs written in an exaggerated imitation of Black speech, performed overwhelmingly by white singers, and sold in enormous quantities. Arthur Collins was the acknowledged master of the style and Edison sold him on that basis.

The record itself is a courtship duet, Collins taking the low comic line and Harlan the melody, over a light ragtime orchestral accompaniment. Musically it is deft; the writing is tight and the two voices interlock in a way that four minutes lets you actually hear. What it is built on is racial caricature, and a modern collector should know that going in rather than discover it a minute into the cylinder.

These records are documents of what a mass American audience was buying in 1909, and they are worth preserving on exactly that ground. Presenting them without comment, or quietly leaving them out of a catalogue, both misrepresent the period.
records.notes: The catalog number rests on a single dealer listing and has not been confirmed against a numerical catalogue or the Edison monthly supplements; treat it as unconfirmed. The title wording also varies between sources in its punctuation.

records.title: American students
records.description:
A band record by the New York Military Band, the name Edison used for the pick-up ensembles of New York players it assembled at West Orange. The band was not a standing organisation with a fixed roster; it was a label credit, and the personnel varied from session to session according to who was available.

Student and college material had a small vogue in the band repertoire of the period, riding on the popularity of college songs and the Ivy League football boom. Pieces of this kind fill the middle of the Amberol lists — competent, cheerful, and forgotten within a decade.

It is worth remembering how physically demanding this repertoire was to record. A band of a dozen or more players had to be arranged in a semicircle round a single horn, with the loud instruments pushed back and the weak ones brought forward, and the whole balance re-set for every title. Nothing could be fixed afterwards.
records.notes: The catalog number comes from a single dealer listing and has not been confirmed against a numerical catalogue; treat it as unconfirmed.

records.title: Morning, noon and night in Vienna
records.description:
Suppé's overture Ein Morgen, ein Mittag, ein Abend in Wien, written in 1844 for a Viennese farce that nobody has staged since, and surviving entirely on the strength of its overture. Along with Poet and Peasant and Light Cavalry it was one of the three Suppé pieces every band in the world could play from memory.

This is a London recording, issued in the American lists under the National (London) Military Band billing. Edison's British studio supplied a great deal of the band material in the Amberol catalogue, and the overtures in particular tend to have come from that source.

The piece is a good test of a four-minute cylinder, because it moves through several tempi and dynamics: a quiet opening, a broad cello-line melody transcribed to euphonium, and a headlong presto finish. On a worn copy the finish is where the trouble shows, since the groove is at its most crowded at the end of the record.
records.notes: The catalog number comes from a single dealer listing and has not been confirmed against a numerical catalogue; treat it as unconfirmed.

records.title: Larboard watch
records.description:
T. Williams's nautical duet of the 1840s, in which two sailors on the middle watch call the hour to each other across the deck. It was a Victorian drawing-room standard on both sides of the Atlantic, and it survived into the recording era because it is genuinely well written for two male voices: the parts cross, answer and finally join in thirds on the refrain.

Edison billed the pairing as Stanley and Gillette — Frank C. Stanley's bass-baritone against the tenor of Henry Burr, whom Edison issued under the pseudonym Irving Gillette. Burr recorded for several companies at once and used a different name at almost every one of them; Stanley, one of the most-recorded bass voices of the era, died in December 1910, which puts a narrow window round any record he is on.

The song's appeal on cylinder was partly technical. Two unaccompanied-sounding voices in close harmony, with only a light orchestral cushion, record cleanly, and the effect of distance the lyric asks for could be produced simply by having one singer step back from the horn.
records.notes: The catalog number comes from a single dealer listing and has not been confirmed against a numerical catalogue; treat it as unconfirmed. "Gillette" is Edison's pseudonym for Henry Burr.

records.title: Two gentlemen from Ireland
records.description:
Stage-Irish comedy of the sort that filled American vaudeville houses and, by extension, the Edison monthly supplements. The Irish-American number was one of the fixed genres of the wax Amberol period, sitting alongside the coon song, the rube sketch and the sentimental ballad, and it ranged from affectionate nostalgia to broad caricature depending on who was writing.

By 1910 the audience for this material was substantially Irish-American itself, which complicates any simple reading of it. The same families who bought sentimental ballads about Killarney bought comic records about drink and brawling, and the performers were frequently Irish-American too.

This entry is included on the strength of a catalogue match for the title and number; the performing credit reported alongside it could not be confirmed, so no artist has been recorded here rather than guess at one.
records.notes: The performer is not recorded here because the attribution could not be confirmed. Title, number and year are supported; the credit is not.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Casey Jones
records.description:
The song that turned a real railroad accident into American folklore. John Luther "Casey" Jones died at the throttle of Illinois Central No. 382 at Vaughan, Mississippi, on 30 April 1900, having stayed on the brake to slow his train while his fireman jumped. The engine-wiper Wallace Saunders is credited with the original ballad; T. Lawrence Seibert and Eddie Newton turned it into a published vaudeville song in 1909, and within a year it was everywhere.

Edison's version is Billy Murray with chorus, and it is one of the defining records of the wax Amberol period — fast, driving, with the chorus punching the refrain. It went out in the June 1910 supplement, at the height of the song's popularity, and it sold accordingly. Murray's diction does a lot of work here: the verses carry actual narrative, and on a four-minute cylinder you get all of it.

The title carried over into the celluloid era as Blue Amberol 1550, which is much the easier of the two to find in playable condition. Collectors who want the wax should expect heavy wear; this was a record bought by people who then played it for visitors.
records.notes: Reissued on Blue Amberol 1550. The wax original is common in poor condition and uncommon in good condition — the usual pattern for a hit title in a soft medium.

records.title: When you and I were young, Maggie
records.description:
James Austin Butterfield's setting of George W. Johnson's poem, written in Canada in the 1860s: an old man addressing his wife at the mill where they courted, with the mill fallen in and the creek dried up. Johnson wrote the words for Maggie Clark, who married him and died within a year. That story is true and it is part of why the song lasted.

Will Oakland sings it, and his voice is the reason to seek this record out. Oakland was a genuine countertenor, not a falsettist, and the sound is strange and affecting in a way that suits a song about looking backwards. Edison marketed the voice frankly as a novelty; the effect on this material is anything but.

Old-favourite ballads of this kind were the ballast of the Amberol catalogue. Every monthly supplement carried a few, they sold slowly and forever, and they are the titles most likely to be found today in a box of cylinders that came out of a family house rather than off a collector's shelf.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Alexander and his clarinet
records.description:
One of the several Alexander songs that circulated just before Irving Berlin's Alexander's Ragtime Band swallowed the name in 1911. The Alexander of these songs is a stock figure of the coon-song repertoire, a Black musician whose playing is irresistible, and the joke is always at his expense as much as in his favour.

What is unusual here is the accompaniment: Collins and Harlan are backed not by the studio orchestra but by the New York Military Band, which gives the record a weight and a snap that the ordinary small-orchestra sides lack, and which lets the clarinet of the title do real work. It is a well-made record, and it is also plainly built on racial caricature; both things are true at once and a catalogue that records only one of them is not much use.

Collins and Harlan were by 1910 the most recorded duet team in the business, working simultaneously for Edison, Victor and Columbia. A collector working through wax Amberols will meet them constantly, and will have to decide what to do about the material. Knowing what is on the cylinder before it goes on the mandrel is the least a catalogue can offer.

records.title: Call me up some rainy afternoon
records.credit_line: Comic song with chorus and orchestra
records.description:
An early Irving Berlin song, published in 1910 when he was still primarily a lyricist working out of Ted Snyder's office, and one of the first to show the conversational, telephone-age wit that would define him. The whole lyric is a woman fending off a suitor by inviting him to call — later, sometime, when it rains.

Ada Jones was the ideal singer for it. The song depends on the gap between what the words say and what the tone says, and Jones could hold that gap open for four minutes. The chorus behind her sharpens the refrain without softening the joke.

The telephone song was a small genre in itself around 1910, the instrument being new enough in ordinary homes to be inherently funny and old enough to be familiar. Records of this kind date themselves precisely, which is much of their value now.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: One sweetly solemn thought
records.description:
Phoebe Cary's verses of 1852, set most often to R. S. Ambrose's tune, a hymn about being one day nearer home that was sung at an extraordinary number of nineteenth-century American funerals and stayed in the repertoire well past the First World War.

The Knickerbocker Quartette give it unaccompanied or nearly so, four male voices in close harmony directly into the horn. This is the configuration that suits a wax cylinder best: no orchestra to muddy the groove, no soloist forcing tone, just four balanced voices at moderate volume.

Sacred quartet cylinders were bought to be played on Sundays and often on Sundays only, which is why they turn up in better condition than almost anything else in the wax Amberol series. If you want to hear what a new four-minute wax cylinder actually sounded like in 1910, a hymn record is usually the honest way to find out.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Silver bell
records.description:
Percy Wenrich's music to Edward Madden's lyric, published in 1910 and one of the biggest of the Indian-intermezzo songs — a craze that ran from Hiawatha in 1903 through Red Wing in 1907 and burned itself out around 1912. The formula was a tom-tom rhythm under a straightforwardly sentimental melody, with a lyric about a Native American couple written by songwriters who had never been west of Hoboken.

Jones and Murray sing it as a duet, and the tune is good enough that the record still works: Wenrich, who also wrote Put On Your Old Grey Bonnet and When You Wore a Tulip, had a gift for a melody that sat well in an untrained voice. Edison put it out in the December 1910 supplement, in time for Christmas.

The Indian song deserves the same plain treatment as the coon song beside it in the catalogue. It is not vicious in the way the dialect comedy is, but it is a costume, and the costume was sold as authenticity. Wenrich's tune outlived the pretence.
records.notes: The Edison labels of the period frequently described such titles as an "Indian love song"; that is a genre marking, not part of the title.

links.label: Edison Amberol 576 at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive

records.title: I'm looking for a nice young fellow who is looking for a nice young girl
records.description:
A title that is itself the joke — the sort of long, self-explaining line that Tin Pan Alley used when it wanted a song to sell itself off a shop counter. Ada Jones sings it as a serio-comic, the music-hall term for a woman's turn that is funny on the surface and slightly rueful underneath.

The serio-comic was Jones's home ground. She had the technique to sing a chorus straight and then undercut it with a spoken half-line, and the four-minute format gave her the room to do that two or three times in one record rather than once.

Edison's 1910 lists are full of this material, and it is worth noticing how much of it is written from a woman's point of view. The audience for parlour records included a great many young working women with their own wages, and the catalogue knew it.

links.label: Edison Amberol 605 at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive

records.title: Come Josephine in my flying machine
records.credit_line: Vocal duet with chorus and orchestra
records.description:
Fred Fisher's music to Alfred Bryan's lyric, published in 1910 and the definitive song of America's first aviation craze. Blériot had crossed the Channel in 1909; by 1911 there were flying meets drawing crowds of a hundred thousand, and a song about taking a girl up in an aeroplane was as topical as popular music got.

Edison's is the Ada Jones and Billy Murray version with chorus, and it is probably the single best-known wax Amberol in existence — the record most likely to be recognised by someone who has never heard of the format. Jones plays Josephine's nerves, Murray plays the pilot's swagger, and the chorus lifts the refrain into the air. The whole thing takes the four minutes it needs.

The song had a long afterlife. It was among the numbers used in the 1997 film Titanic, which put it in front of an audience of tens of millions and made it, briefly, the most famous piece of 1910 popular music in the world. A collector will meet this title constantly and should hold out for a clean copy, since worn ones are everywhere.
records.notes: Very heavily played. On a good copy the chorus entries stay clean; on a worn one they blur into a single band of noise. As with every wax Amberol, never wash it — clean only by dusting the groove with a soft brush.

records.title: Piano man
records.description:
A ragtime song about a piano player, sung by Billy Murray and listed by Edison under the coon-song heading that the company used without embarrassment throughout the wax Amberol years.

The subject — the ragtime pianist as irresistible force — was a fixture of the genre, and it points at something real underneath the caricature. Ragtime was Black music, played in the main by Black musicians, and the songs that white vaudevillians sang about it were simultaneously an acknowledgment of that fact and a way of managing it. Murray sings it straight and fast, without the heavy dialect that Arthur Collins would have applied.

1911 is late in the wax Amberol story. Within eighteen months Edison would announce the Blue Amberol, and the black wax four-minute record would be withdrawn from the lists. Cylinders from the last two years of the series were made in smaller quantities than those from the 1909 boom, and are correspondingly harder to find.

records.title: The old oaken bucket
records.description:
Samuel Woodworth's poem of 1817 — the moss-covered bucket that hung in the well — set to the tune usually credited to George Kiallmark, and by the phonograph era one of the most thoroughly domesticated songs in the American repertoire. It was in every school songbook and every parlour album for the better part of a century.

Songs of this vintage did particular work in the Amberol catalogue. A machine sold to a family had to have something on it for the grandparents, and the monthly supplements always carried a handful of old favourites among the ragtime and the topical comedy. They also sold for years rather than months, which is why so many of them were carried across into the celluloid series.

This one duly reappeared as Blue Amberol 2046. The performing credit on the wax issue could not be confirmed, so none is recorded here.
records.notes: Reissued on Blue Amberol 2046. The performer on the wax issue is not recorded here because the attribution could not be confirmed.

records.title: It's got to be some one I love
records.description:
Ada Jones with chorus in a courtship song of the standard 1911 shape: a verse laying out the terms and a refrain conceding them. The lyric's premise — that the singer will marry, but on her own terms and for affection rather than money — was a reliable formula, and Jones sang a great many variations on it.

Her voice by this date had darkened slightly from the sound of the 1905 records, which suits the material. She was also, by 1911, recording less frantically than in her peak years; the industry was beginning to shift towards younger singers and towards the disc.

The number places this in the last full year of wax Amberol production. Edison announced the Blue Amberol in 1912, and by the end of that year the black wax four-minute cylinder was finished as a commercial product — a five-year format that had been made obsolete twice over, first by celluloid and then by the disc.

records.title: Alexander's ragtime band
records.description:
Irving Berlin's breakthrough, published in March 1911 and within months the most successful popular song America had produced. It is not, strictly, a ragtime number — the melody barely syncopates — but it is a song about ragtime, and it sold something like a million and a half copies of sheet music in its first year.

Billy Murray's Edison version is one of a dozen recordings made in the rush, and Murray's is among the most driven: he takes the refrain at a clip and lands the internal rhymes hard. Berlin's lyric is a barker's pitch — come on and hear, come on and hear — and Murray sings it as one.

Berlin was twenty-three and had been writing songs for four years. The Alexander of the title came out of the same coon-song tradition as the earlier Alexander numbers in this catalogue, and the song has been argued over on that ground ever since; what is not in dispute is that it ended the ragtime era by absorbing it into mainstream popular song. For a collector, a wax Amberol of this title is a chance to hear the biggest hit of the decade in the format it was first bought on.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: The rosary
records.description:
Ethelbert Nevin's setting of Robert Cameron Rogers's poem, published in 1898 and one of the most commercially successful American art songs ever written — the sheet music is reputed to have sold in the millions over thirty years. The hours I spent with thee, dear heart, are as a string of pearls to me: it is a love song in the vocabulary of devotion, which is precisely why it worked in Protestant parlours as readily as Catholic ones.

Elizabeth Spencer sings it with organ rather than orchestra, and the choice matters. An organ gives a wax cylinder a continuous, low-energy background that does not fight the voice for groove space, and the result is one of the more atmospheric records in the late wax Amberol lists.

The title moved to celluloid as Blue Amberol 1525, one of the early numbers in that series, which tells you how confident Edison was of its continued sale. A wax copy is the scarcer object; a Blue Amberol copy is the one you are likely to be offered.
records.notes: Reissued on Blue Amberol 1525. Sources associate this title with both Elizabeth Spencer and the Knickerbocker Quartette personnel; the soprano-and-organ credit recorded here is the reading best supported, but the exact billing on the wax issue is unconfirmed.

records.title: By the dear old river Rhine
records.description:
A Rhineland waltz-ballad of the kind American publishers turned out steadily before 1914, when Germany was still a sentimental homeland to a very large immigrant population rather than an enemy. Songs about the Rhine, the Tyrol and old Heidelberg sold in quantity, and vanished almost overnight in 1917.

Edison lists this as a tenor duet with orchestra, with Albert Campbell as one of the voices. Campbell spent his career in exactly this repertoire — close-harmony duets and quartets, sung slowly and sweetly — and was a founder member of the Peerless Quartet. The identity of his partner on this record could not be confirmed and no second credit has been invented for it.

As a piece of catalogue history the record is a small reminder of how quickly a repertoire can become unsellable. Within six years of this cylinder, Edison and every other American company had quietly withdrawn most of their German-sentimental titles from the lists.
records.notes: Only one of the two singers could be identified. The pairing, and the exact release year, are unconfirmed.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Mandy, come out in the pale moonlight
records.description:
A late wax Amberol, from the final year of the format, sung by Walter Van Brunt — then about twenty and already one of Edison's most-used voices.

The song belongs to the plantation-serenade strand of the coon-song repertoire: a Black suitor calling his sweetheart out into the moonlight, written by white songwriters in stage dialect for a white audience. It is gentler than the knockabout comedy Collins and Harlan specialised in, and that gentleness is its own kind of problem, since it sells a picture of Southern life that was being actively enforced by law and violence at the time the record was made.

Van Brunt sings it without exaggeration, which was becoming the fashion; by 1912 the heavy dialect delivery was starting to sound old. He would go on singing into the electrical era under the name Walter Scanlan, and outlived nearly everyone else in this catalogue.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: That baboon baby dance
records.description:
A Collins and Harlan animal-dance number from the last year of the wax Amberol, riding the 1912 craze for dances named after animals — the turkey trot, the grizzly bear, the bunny hug — which scandalised newspaper editors and clergymen for about two seasons.

The title is the problem, and it is not incidental. Comparing Black dancers to apes was a standing device of American racial caricature, and this song uses it as its central conceit. The music is a competent piece of 1912 ragtime; the premise is what it is. A collector who plays wax Amberols will meet material like this regularly, and the honest thing is to say plainly what is on the cylinder rather than describe it as a novelty dance number and leave it there.

By the number, this belongs to the final months of black wax production. Edison announced the Blue Amberol in 1912 and the celluloid cylinder took over the series from 1501; the wax records above about 1100 had short production runs and are among the harder ones to find.
records.notes: Contains racial caricature in its title and lyric, of a kind common in the 1908-1912 Edison lists.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: When Uncle Joe plays a rag on his old banjo
records.description:
One of the last Collins and Harlan sides in the wax series, and a good example of the plantation-nostalgia strain that ran alongside the harder comic material: an old Black banjo player, a Southern evening, everybody dancing. The banjo in the accompaniment is real and prominent, which makes the record more musically interesting than its lyric deserves.

Songs of this kind were doing a specific cultural job in 1912. They offered a version of the antebellum South as a place of contented music-making, at a moment when the actual South was in the middle of the lynching era and the Great Migration was beginning. That gap between the record and the world is worth holding in mind while listening.

At catalogue number 1117 this is near the end of the wax Amberol run. The series was closed out during 1912 as Edison moved to celluloid, and the highest domestic numbers are scarce simply because they were made for a shrinking market in the months before the format was withdrawn.
records.notes: Plantation-nostalgia material of a kind ubiquitous in the period; the lyric is written in stage dialect.

links.label: Listen at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive (via Calisphere)

records.title: Bonnie Leezie Lindsay
records.credit_line: Character comic song (Scottish) with orchestra accompaniment
records.description:
Harry Lauder, recorded in Edison's London studio and issued in the 12000 block that the company used for its British four-minute cylinders. Lauder was at this date the highest-paid entertainer in the world, and Edison's ability to put him on wax was a genuine competitive advantage in both markets.

The Lauder formula is fully formed here: a Scots courting song delivered in broad Lanarkshire, with the comedy in the timing and the sentiment arriving unannounced in the last chorus. He wrote most of his own material and performed it in a costume — kilt, tam, crooked stick — that fixed an image of Scotland in the Anglophone imagination for fifty years, to the lasting irritation of a good many Scots.

The 12000 series is a distinct numbering block from the American domestic run and a collector should not read across between them. Copies circulated on both sides of the Atlantic, and British-market Lauder cylinders turn up in American collections regularly.
records.notes: Belongs to the British 12000 four-minute block rather than the domestic American numbering. The release year is unconfirmed.

records.title: With sword and lance march
records.description:
Hermann Starke's Mit Schwert und Lanze, a German cavalry march that had entered the international band repertoire alongside Teike's Alte Kameraden, played here by Edison's London band and issued in the British 12000 four-minute series.

The march is built for effect: a hammering introduction, a broad trio, and a return that piles the whole band onto the melody. It suited a four-minute cylinder because there was nothing to cut, and it suited the acoustic horn because it is loud from beginning to end.

The title survived the withdrawal of wax, reappearing on Blue Amberol 23074 — a number in the foreign-recorded block of the celluloid series. That kind of cross-reference is the most reliable way to trace a wax Amberol master through the change of medium, since Edison carried over the recordings it thought would keep selling and quietly abandoned the rest.
records.notes: British 12000 block. Reissued on Blue Amberol 23074; the release year given here is inferred from the numbering and is unconfirmed.

records.title: L'elisir d'amore
records.subtitle: Selection
records.credit_line: Tenor solo in Italian with orchestra
records.description:
One of the small group of Alessandro Bonci cylinders that open the 29000 block, and the reason the block exists. When Edison launched the celluloid Amberol in 1912 he wanted a celebrity tier to set against Victor's Red Seal, and Bonci — a lyric tenor of the front rank, widely held to be the most elegant stylist of his generation — was the name he secured. The Bonci cylinders were priced at a dollar each, against thirty-five cents for an ordinary Blue Amberol, and they were numbered in their own series from 29001.

The repertoire is Donizetti, which was Bonci's core territory: L'elisir d'amore gave him the tenor aria most associated with his voice. What survives on the cylinder is a light, exactly placed tone and an unhurried line, quite unlike the weight Caruso brought to the same music.

These six numbers are the hinge of the whole Royal Purple story. When Edison stopped adding to the 75-cent classical 28000 series in 1918, he restarted the dollar celebrity idea in the same 29000 block, this time on purple-dyed celluloid — so the Bonci numbers sit immediately below the Royal Purples proper and are often catalogued with them.
records.notes: Whether the Bonci numbers 29001-29006 were themselves issued in purple or in ordinary blue celluloid is disputed between sources; the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive catalogues this one as an Edison Royal Purple Amberol. The specific aria is not confirmed — dealer descriptions give only "from Elisir d'Amore" — and the release year is inferred from the launch of the celebrity block.

links.label: Edison Royal Purple Amberol 29002 at the UCSB Cylinder Audio Archive

records.title: Aloha oe
records.subtitle: Farewell to thee
records.credit_line: Soprano with male quartet and orchestra
records.description:
The first of the Royal Purples proper, and a good illustration of what the series actually was. Edison had stopped adding to his 75-cent classical 28000 cylinders in 1918 and restarted the celebrity idea in the 29000 block, on cylinders dyed a deep purple instead of the usual blue, at a dollar apiece. The colour was the whole marketing proposition: a customer could see at a glance that the record on the mandrel was the expensive one.

The repertoire was not, in the event, mostly grand opera. Frieda Hempel was a Metropolitan coloratura of the first rank, but here she sings Queen Liliuokalani's Aloha Oe with the Criterion Quartet behind her — a Hawaiian song that had been a mainland hit since the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition set off a craze for the islands' music. Celebrity singers in simple material was the formula, and it was a shrewd one.

Collectors should understand what they are hearing. Almost every Royal Purple is an acoustic dubbing: the performance was recorded for a Diamond Disc, and the cylinder was made by playing the disc back and re-recording it through a horn onto the cylinder master. The fidelity is therefore a generation removed from the original, and noticeably duller than a directly recorded cylinder of the same date.
records.provenance: Dubbed acoustically from the Edison Diamond Disc master.

records.title: My old Kentucky home
records.credit_line: Soprano with male quartet and orchestra
records.description:
Stephen Foster's song of 1853, sung by Frieda Hempel with the Criterion Quartet — the companion number to her Aloha Oe and, like it, taken from an Edison Diamond Disc and dubbed onto the cylinder.

Foster wrote the song in the plantation-melody idiom he had made his own, and it has been sung ever since in versions that steadily sand down its origins: the original lyric's use of a racial slur was quietly replaced with "people" over the course of the twentieth century, and Kentucky adopted it as the state song in 1928. What Hempel offers is the fully genteel version, a European-trained coloratura treating Foster as art song.

That treatment was deliberate. Hempel was in the middle of her Jenny Lind period, giving costumed recreations of the Swedish soprano's American tour of 1850-52, and Foster's songs belonged to exactly that programme. The Royal Purple series is the recorded residue of that idea — celebrity voices, familiar tunes, premium price, purple celluloid.
records.provenance: Dubbed acoustically from the Edison Diamond Disc master.

records.title: Valse sentimentale
records.description:
Albert Spalding playing a sentimental waltz, and one of the most talked-about numbers in the whole Royal Purple series for a reason that has nothing to do with the music: it is generally held to be the only Royal Purple dubbed from a Diamond Disc that Edison never actually issued as a disc. The cylinder is therefore the sole published form of that performance.

Spalding matters in his own right. He was the first American-born violinist to establish an international reputation on equal terms with the European school, and he was an Edison exclusive artist through the Diamond Disc years, which is why his records are all on Edison and nowhere else.

The Royal Purples ran from 29007 to roughly 29080, issued between about 1918 and 1921, after which the celebrity titles reverted to ordinary blue celluloid and the purple series was closed. Seventy-odd numbers over three years, all of them expensive and none of them big sellers, makes the Royal Purple one of the scarcer things a cylinder collector can go looking for.
records.provenance: Dubbed acoustically from a Diamond Disc master that is generally reported never to have been issued as a disc.
records.notes: The precise release year is inferred from the position of the number within the 29007-29080 run and is unconfirmed.
